items.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997
items.q: Bob Crosby’s Bobcats with Bob Haggart, which was really nice, great arrangement that he did

ctx.x: And kind of, you are just about my age, and I remember listening to certain, a lot of pop music and then being greatly affected by groups like Blood, Sweat & Tears and stuff. Was that something — did you share that?

Well yeah, I mean not them specifically. Basically how I got into listening to jazz was I guess through my older brother. I mean our parents had some 78s that belonged to I guess their parents. And it was a very mixed bag. But in it were some kind of interesting things. Nothing great, but I mean like there was something by “The Georgians” like this little combo from the 20s, and Bob Crosby’s Bobcats with Bob Haggart, which was really nice, great arrangement that he did, you know, some jazz things. And that just…

Beiderbecke Story on Columbia, which George Avakian did. So when I was 10, 11, 12, I was really absorbed in that. And pretty soon thereafter we were listening to Clifford Brown and Dizzy Gillespie. And one thing, this was in the late 50s — well early 60s I guess. One advantage that we had was that a lot of these people were still around then. So I could hear them. I only heard Louis once, but it was just a completely mind-altering experience. And Duke Ellington I was fortunate to hear when he still had his band…

items.title: Bob Haggart interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995
items.q: Dan Barrett, Jon-Erik Kellso, Randy Sandke, Harry Allen. Now there are a lot more than that, but they happen to be the ones that I’ve been working with lately.

ctx.x: Is there anything we can do to kind of create that respect for this art form, right here in the United States?

Gee, I wish I could answer that one. But you’re doing what you can by having these archives and trying to expose the kids to letting them hear some of the stuff live. I’ve been playing a few elementary schools and high schools and little kids love it. It’s amazing how little kids, first graders, second graders, third graders, they come in and they just get so excited. They jump all around you know, and if you could get them at that age, that’s—but how you going to do it, because there aren’t enough musicians…
play. You’ve got to have places where you can be lousy, to start. And in those days, you could. You could play rotten and they thought it was marvelous.
